faqs.question: Can I do Govardhan puja without cow dung?
faqs.answer: Yes. A hill of stiff wheat-flour (atta) dough, potter's clay, or the Annakut food itself heaped into a mound all serve, and the rest of the vidhi stays the same. Many flat-dwellers use 1 kg of atta on a steel thali.

faqs.question: Should Govardhan puja be done in the morning or the evening?
faqs.answer: Both are traditional; families differ, and many shape the hill in the morning and worship in the afternoon or evening. In 2027 the day is Saturday 30 October, so check your local panchang for your city's window.

faqs.question: How many times do you go around the Govardhan?
faqs.answer: Seven rounds is the common count, walked clockwise with the hill on your right. If the hill sits against a wall, carry the thali around instead.

faqs.question: What should I do with the Govardhan after the puja?
faqs.answer: Leave it until evening, then put a dung hill into a garden bed or compost, compost atta dough once the cotton and roli are picked off, and return clay to a plant pot.

faqs.question: Can women perform Govardhan puja at home?
faqs.answer: Yes. In William Crooke's 1896 records from Punjab and the North-Western Provinces, it is the women of the house who build the Govardhan.

faqs.question: Is a pandit needed for Govardhan puja?
faqs.answer: No. It is a household rite: water, roli, rice, flowers, incense, a diya and food, followed by the parikrama and aarti, all of which a family can do on its own.

faqs.question: What do you feed a cow on Govardhan puja?
faqs.answer: The first portion of the day's cooking, usually rotis with jaggery or a bundle of green fodder. In a city, take it to a gaushala before 9 AM.

faqs.question: Is cow dung safe to handle indoors?
faqs.answer: Handle it with gloves. A 2025 study of 10 Bangladeshi households detected 220 potential pathogen species in household cow dung, including E. coli and Salmonella, so keep children's hands off and wash before touching food.

faqs.question: How big should a home Govardhan be?
faqs.answer: About 30 cm long is plenty for a family, with three to five small mounds around it. For the 20-minute short form, a palm-sized hill works.

faqs.question: Can the Annakut be eaten after the puja?
faqs.answer: Yes. Once offered, the Annakut becomes prasad and is shared with the family and sent to neighbours; keep it untasted until it has been offered.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Govardhan Puja Vidhi at Home: Steps, Samagri and a Flat-Friendly Version

Govardhan puja vidhi at home comes down to five acts on the morning after Diwali, which in 2027 is Saturday 30 October: shape a small Govardhan hill, feed a cow before the family eats, set out the Annakut, worship the hill with water, flowers, lamp and food, then walk around it, commonly seven times. The full order below takes about two hours; a short form takes 20 minutes (both our estimates).

Many people now do this puja in a flat and send greetings the same morning. SubhSandesh has no Diwali usage data yet, so the nearest measure is Raksha Bandhan 2026 (n = 89, a different festival): 11.2% of greeting pages were built after the festival had passed, and 48.3% of all shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone. This guide covers the vidhi, the samagri, four substitutes for an apartment, and how regions differ.

## What a Govardhan puja involves

Govardhan Puja honours the hill in Braj that, in the Krishna story, sheltered the cowherds from Indra's storm, and it falls on Kartik Shukla Pratipada, the first lunar day after Diwali's new moon. F. S. Growse's [Mathura: A District Memoir (1883)](https://archive.org/details/mathurdistrict00growrich) notes that the hill was "more frequently designated the Anna-kut" in earlier literature, which is why the food offering and the hill share a name.

Growse's calendar of Mathura festivals lists Kartik Sudi 1 as Anna-kut, with "the same observances as at Gobardhan, but on a smaller scale." That is still the logic of a home puja: you build a small hill where you live and do at your door what pilgrims do at the real one.

## Govardhan puja samagri: what to gather by Friday night

Quantities are our estimates for a family of four and a hill about 30 cm long; the last column is what to use when the traditional item is out of reach.

| Samagri group | Traditional item and amount | Used in step | Apartment substitute |
|---|---|---|---|
| The hill | 2–3 kg fresh cow dung | 2 | 1 kg wheat-flour (atta) dough, or 1 kg potter's clay |
| Hill decoration | 10–15 grass stems, a pinch of cotton wool, 5 sugarcane pieces, 2 marigold strings | 3 | Coriander stalks, cotton buds, one sugarcane cut into 5 |
| Cow's portion | 2 rotis with jaggery, or a bundle of green fodder | 4 | The same food taken to a gaushala, or a donation there |
| Annakut | 5–7 vegetarian dishes cooked that morning, plus kheel and batasha | 5 | 3 dishes from the day's regular cooking |
| Puja thali | 1 ghee diya, roli, rice, incense, a lota of water, a wooden churn-staff (mathani) | 6–7 | A steel plate under the diya; a wooden ladle for the churn-staff |

## Govardhan puja kaise kare: the home vidhi in 8 steps

The order follows household practice recorded in northern India in the 1890s, adjusted for a modern home. Families who worship in the afternoon or evening can shift every step.

### 1. Bathe and clear a spot

Bathe early, with oil if that is your custom, and sweep a patch of courtyard, balcony or floor about 60 cm square. Allow 15 minutes, and lay a jute sack down first if working indoors.

### 2. Shape the reclining Govardhan

William Crooke's [The Popular Religion and Folk-Lore of Northern India, Vol. 2 (1896)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/43682) quotes a Punjab account of women making "a Govardhan of cowdung, which consists of Krishna lying on his back", ringed by little loaves of dung for mountains and dung balls for cattle. Shape the reclining figure first, about 30 cm long, then add three to five small mounds around it and a handful of marble-sized balls for the herd. Give it 30 minutes.

### 3. Dress the hill

In the same account, stems of grass with tufts of cotton or rag on top stand in for trees, and a churn-staff, five white sugarcanes, parched rice and a lamp go on the figure, with the lamp in the middle. Add the marigolds last; the whole step takes about 10 minutes.

### 4. Feed a cow first

The first portion of the day's food traditionally goes to a cow before anyone in the house eats: two rotis with jaggery, or green fodder. In a city, take it to a gaushala or a cow you know on your street, and go before 9 AM on 30 October, since many families have the same plan.

### 5. Set out the Annakut

Arrange the dishes in a semicircle before the hill, sweets nearest. Allow 10 minutes, and keep the food untasted until it is offered, because it becomes prasad afterwards.

### 6. Worship the hill

Sprinkle water on the figure, apply roli and a few grains of rice, offer flowers, wave the incense and the lit diya, then offer the Annakut by touching a tulsi leaf to each dish. About 15 minutes is enough.

### 7. Walk the parikrama

Walk clockwise around the hill, keeping it on your right, commonly for seven rounds, singing as you go. If the hill sits against a wall in a small flat, carry the thali around it instead, which takes about 10 minutes.

### 8. Aarti, prasad and taking the hill down

Close with an aarti, share the Annakut as prasad and send a plate to two or three neighbours. In the evening, put dung into a garden bed or compost, pick the cotton and roli off atta dough before composting it, and return clay to a plant pot.

## Apartment-friendly Govardhan puja: four substitutes and one hygiene rule

Fresh cow dung is hard to find in a high-rise, and it does not belong on a kitchen counter. A 2025 study of 10 rural households in Sirajganj, Bangladesh, by [Nguyen and colleagues in Applied and Environmental Microbiology](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12175521), detected 220 potential pathogen species in household cow dung (38 in dung alone, 182 shared with floor soil), with E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Salmonella enterica among the most abundant.

We read only the abstract, and it studied floor sealing, not puja hills, but the lesson carries over: wear gloves, keep toddlers' hands off the hill, and wash before you touch the Annakut. These four substitutes keep the vidhi intact:

- **Atta dough hill.** 1 kg of wheat flour kneaded stiff holds a reclining shape on a steel thali.
- **Clay hill.** 1 kg of potter's clay, or garden soil mixed with water, and it goes back into a plant pot afterwards.
- **The Annakut as the hill.** Heap rice or the cooked dishes into a mound and worship that, which fits Growse's note that the hill was once called Anna-kut.
- **Picture and tulsi.** Place a picture of Krishna lifting Govardhan beside the tulsi pot, and walk the parikrama around the pot.

On a balcony, stand the diya on a steel plate. The Telangana Fire Department's [public safety advisory for Diwali (18 October 2025)](https://fire.telangana.gov.in/WebSite/Images/PublicSafetyAdvisoryforDiwali2025.pdf) asks for diyas on stable surfaces away from curtains or decorations, and never left unattended.

## Regional variations in the Govardhan puja vidhi

None of these is the single correct version, so follow your elders where they differ. Crooke's 1896 survey records three, and Growse adds a fourth:

- **Punjab:** the reclining dung Krishna described above; cowherds are called in to salute it and are fed rice and sweets, and no one eats, cuts or presses sugarcane until the Brahman has tasted it. The bullocks have their horns dyed and are fed extra.
- **North-Western Provinces (today's Uttar Pradesh):** women build a small mud hut on a platform outside the house with images of Gauri and Ganesha, set beside it the parched grain the girls offered on Diwali night, lay thorny grass nearby and wave a rice pounder around it while blessing relatives.
- **Cawnpore (Kanpur), the "Dang" Diwali:** cowherds worship a little heap of dung decorated with cotton, then go house to house dancing to two sticks and a drum, collecting grain, cloth or money.
- **Mathura city, 1883:** the Anna-kut on the first day of Kartik's bright fortnight repeats the Gobardhan observances on a smaller scale.

In Gujarat the same Saturday is Bestu Varas, the New Year, and in Maharashtra Bali Pratipada, so a smaller Govardhan there is a variation, not a lapse.

## How long it takes, and a 20-minute short form

Added up, the eight steps run about 125 minutes from bath to prasad, and shaping the hill is the longest single step at 30 minutes. No priest is needed; in two of Crooke's three accounts, the women of the house build the hill.

If the morning is short, a 20-minute form keeps every essential act:

- 5 minutes: a palm-sized atta hill on a steel thali.
- 5 minutes: water, roli, flowers, incense and the diya.
- 2 minutes: one dish from breakfast offered as the Annakut.
- 5 minutes: seven rounds of the thali.
- 3 minutes: aarti and prasad.

## Where SubhSandesh fits, and where it does not

SubhSandesh is not a puja tool, and nothing on it builds a Govardhan. It covers the greeting for one person who is not at your puja this year, and the day after Diwali is when late greetings go out (11.2% of Raksha Bandhan 2026 pages were built after the day, n = 89).

For that one person, the [interactive Diwali card on SubhSandesh](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali) lets them light a diya at their door with your tag on it, light sky lanterns holding up to six of your photos, and open your letter from a shagun liffafa. It takes about five minutes to make, has love, family and friend modes, and opens as a private link in any browser with no app; an average SubhSandesh page is opened 11.1 times, so they can return to it later. It has no Govardhan scene, so describe your Annakut in the letter.

Because Govardhan Puja shares its date with the Gujarati New Year, a couple marking both could use the [Capsule page, where you each write sealed predictions for the year](https://subhsandesh.in/capsule) and open them together a year later. It is a couples template, not a festival one. Neither page replaces a phone call to elders who keep the puja the old way.
